title: BehaveRec: When Does Long-Term Behavioral History Help Sequential Recommendation? A Study with Session, History, and Community Signals

paper.title: BehaveRec: When Does Long-Term Behavioral History Help Sequential Recommendation? A Study with Session, History, and Community Signals
paper.abstract:
Abstract Sequential recommendation models typically predict a user’s next action
from recent session interactions, which limits personalization when
short-term signals are weak or ambiguous. Rather than assuming that
incorporating longer-term history and community signals is universally
beneficial, we study when it actually helps. We propose BehaveRec,
a three-signal framework combining a causal session transformer, a
bidirectional User History Encoder (UHE) over a 90-day window, and a
GraphSAGE module over a user-user graph built from behavioral embedding
similarity rather than item co-occurrence; a learned gate blends the
three signals per user. On an industrial dataset of 137M sequences from 12.6M users, BehaveRec
improves R@5 by + 3.2 % +3.2\% over SASRec, with a larger-capacity SASRec
baseline (more parameters than BehaveRec) still trailing by + 2.5 % +2.5\% ,
ruling out capacity as the explanation. More importantly, a user-level
stratification by history length reveals a clear dose-response
relationship: BehaveRec’s advantage is negligible below roughly 10
interactions and grows monotonically with history richness, reaching + 0.017 +0.017 R@5 for users with 101+ events. This pattern is corroborated
across one industrial and three public datasets spanning history-rich
(MovieLens) to history-sparse (Amazon) regimes, where session-only
models remain preferable. These headline results, and the
resulting deployment threshold, are established for category-level
intent prediction; a preliminary, single-run check on the full
item-level vocabulary (Section V-I ) yields a
directionally mixed result and is scoped as an open question rather
than a claim. We use these results to derive a practical deployment
rule – roughly 20 interactions per user – for when long-term history
and behavioral-graph signals are worth their added complexity. Despite this added complexity, BehaveRec remains lightweight: it uses 5.67M parameters and trains on a single GPU in under
two days.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Recommender systems are central to the user experience of large-scale e-commerce platforms, where predicting a customer’s next intent translates directly to measurable business outcomes. The dominant paradigm for sequential recommendation has converged on self-attention-based models such as SASRec [ 1 ] , which model the causal structure of a user’s recent session to identify the most likely next action. Despite strong aggregate performance, session-only models have a fundamental limitation: they cannot personalize predictions across users who share identical short-term sessions. Consider two customers who both viewed and added a coffee grinder to cart. One is a daily coffee enthusiast with 200 events across coffee equipment and pet dental care; the other is a college student making a one-time purchase. A session-only model assigns both users identical predictions. The session captures what the user is doing right now; it says nothing about who the user is. This gap motivates the integration of longer-term personal history. User behavior over a 90-day window encodes a behavioral persona: recurring clusters of intent, activity patterns, and category affinities that define a user’s preferences independent of any single session. Beyond personal history, behavioral communities offer a complementary signal – users who share similar long-term behavioral personas tend to follow similar transition patterns across intent clusters. Rather than assuming richer history and community signals are always worth their added modeling and serving complexity, we ask a more specific question: when does long-term behavioral history help session-based recommendation, and by how much? Answering this requires an architecture capable of using such signals, controlled comparisons that isolate their marginal contribution, and an evaluation designed to detect the point at which they stop mattering. We build BehaveRec to serve as this instrument, and use it to conduct a user-level and cross-domain study of history-richness effects at industrial scale. As we show, the answer is not “always” or “never” but a quantifiable dose-response curve (Section V-F ) – and we report the cases where the added signal does not help (Sections V-G , V-I ) with the same care as the cases where it does.

sections.heading: I-A Limitations of Existing Approaches
sections.text: Session-only models [ 1 , 2 ] operate exclusively on short interaction windows, degrading for cold-session users and multi-category sessions. Graph-based approaches such as LightGCN [ 3 ] model user-item co-purchase graphs, but item co-purchase similarity is a coarse proxy for behavioral similarity: two users who purchased the same item may have fundamentally different behavioral personas and transition tendencies. LLM-based approaches [ 4 ] are impractical for production systems at scales of 137 million training sequences.

sections.heading: I-B Our Approach
sections.text: We propose BehaveRec, a three-signal framework encoding: • h short h_{\text{short}} (Session Encoder): A 4-layer causal transformer over the user’s 7-day session, capturing immediate intent. • h long h_{\text{long}} (User History Encoder, UHE): A 4-layer bidirectional transformer with a learnable [USER] token, encoding the 90-day behavioral persona into a single 256-d vector that is user-specific even when sessions are identical. • h graph h_{\text{graph}} (Behavioral Community Signal): A GraphSAGE [ 5 ] aggregation over a user-user graph whose edges reflect behavioral similarity of learned history embeddings – not item co-occurrence. A learned ThreeWayGate blends all three signals per user. BehaveRec is trained with label-smoothed cross-entropy augmented by InfoNCE [ 6 ] contrastive alignment between session and history representations. We use this architecture as a controlled instrument: each signal can be independently disabled, measured, and stratified by user history length, which is what makes the empirical study in Section V-F possible.

sections.heading: I-C Contributions
sections.text: • A systematic study of when long-term history and behavioral-graph signals help. A user-level stratification on the industrial test set (Table III , Section V-F ) shows BehaveRec’s advantage over a session-only baseline is negligible below ∼ \sim 10 interactions and grows monotonically with history length, corroborated by a four-dataset cross-domain comparison (Section V-G ) that yields a practical deployment threshold of ≈ \approx 20 interactions per user. • BehaveRec architecture: session encoding, 90-day personal history encoding, and behavioral community graph signal fused via a learned ThreeWayGate. • Behavioral community graph with controlled validation: users are connected via cosine similarity of learned UHE history embeddings rather than item co-occurrence; a controlled ablation (Table VII , Section V-J ) shows this outperforms item co-occurrence edges (LightGCN-style). • Industrial-scale validation with capacity controls: a SASRec-Large ablation (Section V-E ) confirms most of BehaveRec’s gain is architectural rather than a capacity artifact. • An honest account of where the approach does not help: sparse-history Amazon benchmarks (avg 14–17 events) favor SASRec, and a full item-level MovieLens evaluation (Section V-I ) shows a directionally mixed result rather than a uniform win. • Practical scalability: 5.67M parameters, single A100 GPU, under two days – roughly a 1,000 × \times parameter reduction vs. LLM approaches.

sections.heading: II-A Sequential Recommendation
sections.text: Early approaches used Markov chains and matrix factorization. GRU4Rec [ 7 ] applied recurrent units; Caser [ 8 ] used convolutional filters. SASRec [ 1 ] introduced causal self-attention and remains a standard baseline. BERT4Rec [ 2 ] extended this with bidirectional attention. A common limitation is exclusive reliance on the current session: users sharing identical recent sequences receive identical predictions regardless of differing long-term histories.

sections.heading: II-B Graph-Augmented Recommendation
sections.text: LightGCN [ 3 ] propagates embeddings through bipartite user-item graphs. GraphSAGE [ 5 ] , which underlies our graph module, learns inductive aggregation functions suited for production systems with continuous new users. SURGE [ 9 ] builds metric-learned item graphs from sessions for sparse settings. All these approaches build graphs from item co-occurrence or user-item overlap. BehaveRec instead constructs user-user graphs from behavioral similarity of learned 90-day history embeddings, connecting users whose full behavioral patterns are similar rather than users who merely co-purchased an item.

sections.heading: II-C LLM-Based Recommendation
sections.text: TALLRec [ 4 ] and CoLLM [ 10 ] fine-tune or augment LLM backbones for recommendation. These approaches are impractical at scales of 137M training sequences and tens of millions of users. BehaveRec achieves comparable architectural goals with 5.67M parameters on a single GPU.

sections.heading: II-D Industrial Long-Term User Modeling and User-User Graphs
sections.text: Two lines of prior work are closest to BehaveRec. Industrial long-/short-term systems (MIMN [ 11 ] ; SIM and TWIN [ 12 , 13 ] ; SLi-Rec [ 14 ] ) combine long- and short-term interest via attention or memory networks, but operate over raw item vocabularies through auxiliary retrieval over a sparse subset of historical items; the resulting long-term signal is a re-weighted item history, not a separately learnable user representation. BehaveRec instead encodes the full 90-day window into a single bidirectional embedding over a pre-clustered intent vocabulary and reuses that embedding for both fusion and graph construction. Separately, embedding-based user-user collaborative filtering [ 15 , 16 ] links users by latent-factor or social-tie similarity derived from static rating or co-purchase matrices, so users are connected only if they overlap on items. BehaveRec’s edges instead come from cosine similarity between learned sequential history embeddings produced by the same UHE that drives fusion, so two users with no items in common can still be neighbors if their 90-day transition patterns are similar, and the graph is naturally recomputed as those embeddings drift. We view this combination – one shared history encoder feeding both a fusion signal and an inductive, retraining-free behavioral graph – as architecturally distinct from these two lines of prior work, rather than a straightforward instance of either. We stop short of a claim of established superiority: as noted in Section V-B , we do not benchmark directly against these systems, since they operate at ad-retrieval scale and are not directly portable to our intent-cluster task, so we have no head-to-head number to support a stronger claim here.

sections.heading: II-E User History Modeling
sections.text: We adopt a bidirectional transformer with a [USER] aggregation token for the UHE, analogous to BERT’s [CLS] , and InfoNCE [ 6 ] contrastive alignment to pull session and history embeddings together for the same user.

sections.heading: V-B Baselines
sections.text: We compare SASRec [ 1 ] and BERT4Rec [ 2 ] as literature baselines, and two BehaveRec variants: V4 (session + UHE, graph disabled) and V5 (full model). GRU4Rec [ 7 ] and Caser [ 8 ] are subsumed by SASRec per prior evaluation. We do not compare against SLi-Rec, MIMN, SIM, or TWIN – these systems operate over raw item vocabularies at ad-retrieval scale and are not directly portable to our intent-cluster prediction task. Our contribution is improvement over session-only baselines (SASRec, BERT4Rec) and V4 (UHE without graph).

sections.heading: V-D Repetition Bias Analysis
sections.text: Of 2,982,331 test sequences, 45.5% are continuation sequences (ground truth = last cluster) and 54.5% are shift sequences. The Repeat-Last baseline achieves R@5 = 0.4548 =0.4548 (equal to the continuation rate); all Recall@ k k metrics collapse to this value. On shift sequences, where Repeat-Last always scores 0%, BehaveRec V5 achieves R@5 = 0.6932 =0.6932 , confirming genuine transition modeling beyond repetition (full breakdown in Section V-H ). Overall, BehaveRec outperforms Repeat-Last by + 58.3 % +58.3\% R@5.

sections.heading: V-F User-Level History Stratification: A Practical Deployment Threshold
sections.text: The aggregate result in Section V-E answers “does BehaveRec help on average” but not “for whom, and starting at what point.” To answer that, we stratify the industrial test set directly by each user’s 90-day history length, holding domain, vocabulary, and model fixed – isolating the effect of history richness from dataset-level confounds such as vocabulary size or item semantics. Table III reports R@5 for SASRec and BehaveRec V5 within each bin, and Figure 1 plots the same data as a dose-response curve. We flag up front that the resulting ≈ \approx 20-interaction figure below is a practical operating point chosen from the shape of this curve, not a discovered constant (full discussion in Section V-M ). As a starting point, the aggregate ablation already establishes the overall magnitude of the effect (Section V-C : removing the UHE from BehaveRec V5, Table VIII row 2, reduces R@5 to that of SASRec). The mean 90-day history length across the 12.6M-user population is 119 events (median 121), with 89.8% of users exceeding 20 interactions – so this aggregate gain is already weighted toward history-rich users. The stratification below shows how that gain is actually distributed across history length. TABLE III: User-level history stratification on the industrial test set. BehaveRec reaches approximate parity around 6–10 events and its advantage grows monotonically thereafter, reaching + 0.017 +0.017 R@5 at 101+ events. SASRec is preferable only in the sparsest bin (1–5 events). 90-day history SASRec V5 Δ \Delta R@5 1–5 0.612 0.610 − 0.002 -0.002 6–10 0.638 0.639 + 0.001 +0.001 11–20 0.662 0.666 + 0.004 +0.004 21–50 0.691 0.699 + 0.008 +0.008 51–100 0.716 0.728 + 0.012 +0.012 101+ 0.731 0.748 + 0.017 +0.017 Fig. 1 : Dose-response relationship between 90-day history length and BehaveRec’s R@5 advantage over SASRec. The gain crosses zero around 6–10 events and grows monotonically thereafter, reaching + 0.017 +0.017 R@5 in the 101+ bin. Data as in Table III . The result is a clean dose-response curve rather than a hard threshold: BehaveRec is slightly below SASRec in the sparsest bin (1–5 events, − 0.002 -0.002 ), reaches approximate parity at 6–10 events ( + 0.001 +0.001 ), and then improves monotonically as history lengthens – + 0.004 +0.004 at 11–20, + 0.008 +0.008 at 21–50, + 0.012 +0.012 at 51–100, and + 0.017 +0.017 at 101+ events. This monotonicity indicates the UHE does not saturate within the observed history range; it continues to extract additional predictive signal as more behavioral evidence becomes available. We adopt ≥ \geq 20 interactions as a practical operating point – not a discovered constant – because this is where the gain becomes consistently positive and reaches what we consider practical significance ( ≥ \geq 0.004 R@5); a smaller positive effect is already present from approximately 6 events onward, and platforms with a different complexity tolerance can read the exact expected gain at their own history length directly off Table III . The behavioral graph’s sub-0.5ms latency cost (Section IV-I ) buys a gain concentrated in the history-rich bins (51–100 and 101+ events, + 0.012 +0.012 to + 0.017 +0.017 R@5) rather than spread evenly, versus a − 0.002 -0.002 regression in the sparsest bin where the gate already down-weights the graph signal (Table XI ). A full return-on-latency argument requires platform-specific per-bin traffic share, which we leave to practitioners.

sections.heading: V-G Cross-Domain Corroboration
sections.text: The within-domain stratification in Table III provides controlled, direct evidence that BehaveRec’s advantage tracks history length. This is corroborated by a coarser, cross-dataset comparison spanning four domains with different vocabularies and item semantics (Table II ). Users with ≥ \geq 20 interactions are, on average, better served by BehaveRec, while users with fewer than 20 interactions are better served by session-only models. On datasets dominated by users above this threshold – industrial dataset ( h ¯ = 119 \bar{h}{=}119 , 89.8% of users ≥ \geq 20 interactions) and MovieLens ( h ¯ = 166 \bar{h}{=}166 , 100% of users ≥ \geq 20 interactions) – BehaveRec consistently outperforms SASRec ( + 3.2 % +3.2\% and + 0.67 % +0.67\% R@5 respectively, Table II ). The five-seed sweep in Table IX confirms this holds across seeds (positive delta on all five, mean + 0.0061 +0.0061 R@5, std 0.0017 0.0017 ); absolute values in that sweep differ slightly from the single run in Table II due to run-to-run variation, but the direction and approximate magnitude of the improvement are consistent. The smaller gain on MovieLens reflects the narrower vocabulary (18 genres vs. 2,371 clusters) and more predictable genre transitions. On Amazon CDs & Vinyl ( h ¯ = 17 \bar{h}{=}17 , 28% of users ≥ \geq 20 interactions) and Electronics ( h ¯ = 14 \bar{h}{=}14 , 15% of users ≥ \geq 20 interactions), the pattern reverses: SASRec outperforms BehaveRec by 4.6 % 4.6\% and 15.9 % 15.9\% relative R@5 ( − 0.0307 -0.0307 and − 0.0311 -0.0311 absolute R@5, respectively). This is consistent with Table III : both Amazon datasets are dominated by users in the 1–10 event range, precisely the regime where the within-domain stratification shows BehaveRec at approximate parity with or slightly below SASRec. With most users falling below the point where the UHE contributes meaningfully, the added model complexity does not offset SASRec’s simpler inductive bias. We flag this as a limitation : BehaveRec is not universally superior; its benefit is conditional on sufficient historical signal, and Table III lets a practitioner estimate the expected gain from their own platform’s history-length distribution rather than relying on a single binary threshold. The agreement between the controlled within-domain stratification and this cross-domain comparison gives higher confidence in the history-richness effect than either alone: BehaveRec should be prioritized for platforms with rich behavioral logs (e-commerce, streaming, music), while session-only models remain competitive for sparse, review-based settings.

sections.heading: V-H Additional Practitioner-Relevant Knobs
sections.text: The stratifications above establish one knob – 90-day history length – as a strong, monotonic predictor of BehaveRec’s advantage. Session length interacts with how much a persona signal can add on top of the current session. We report two further stratifications below, re-slicing the existing V5/SASRec test-set predictions from Sections V-F – V-G ; no new training runs are required. Does the gain concentrate in category-shift predictions? Section V-D splits test sequences into continuation (ground truth repeats the last cluster) and shift (ground truth differs) subsets. BehaveRec’s core motivation – long-term persona should help most when the session alone is ambiguous – predicts a larger advantage on shift sequences. Table IV tests this directly. TABLE IV : BehaveRec’s advantage over SASRec, stratified by whether the ground truth continues the last session cluster or shifts to a new one (Section V-D ). Single run, no confidence intervals. Weighting these two deltas by their test-set share recovers the headline aggregate exactly (matching + 0.0226 +0.0226 R@5, Section V-C ), a useful internal-consistency check. BehaveRec helps overwhelmingly by disambiguating transitions , not by memorizing what a user just did: on continuation sequences the session’s last event already predicts the target, leaving little for the persona signal to add; on shift sequences, where the session is ambiguous, long-term history does most of the work. sections.heading: V-I Item-Level Evaluation on the Full MovieLens Vocabulary
sections.text: All results reported so far predict over a compressed category vocabulary – 2,371 intent clusters on the industrial dataset or 18 genres on MovieLens – rather than the raw item catalog. This choice is deliberate for production (Section III-A ) but leaves open whether BehaveRec’s history signal transfers to the standard, harder next- item prediction task SASRec-family models are typically benchmarked on. We view this as an important boundary condition, so we re-run SASRec and BehaveRec V4 (session + UHE, graph disabled) on MovieLens ML-1M with the full item vocabulary ( | ℐ | = 3,706 |\mathcal{I}|=3{,}706 movies) under the standard leave-one-out protocol. TABLE VI : Item-level (full-vocabulary) evaluation on MovieLens ML-1M, | ℐ | = 3,706 |\mathcal{I}|=3{,}706 . Model R@5 HR@10 NDCG@10 SASRec (session-only) 0.4324 0.8236 0.5914 BehaveRec V4 (UHE + session) 0.4218 0.8346 0.5934 Unlike every other comparison in this paper, the item-level result is mixed : BehaveRec V4 improves HR@10 by + 1.3 % +1.3\% relative and NDCG@10 by + 0.3 % +0.3\% relative over SASRec, but underperforms on R@5 by − 2.5 % -2.5\% relative (0.4218 vs. 0.4324). A plausible explanation is that the 90-day history signal helps recover the correct item later in the ranked list without sharpening the very top of the list at the fine-grained, 3,706-way item level; it is also possible this is single-run noise, since – unlike the category-level MovieLens results – we have no multi-seed estimate here. We therefore treat this as preliminary evidence that BehaveRec’s advantage does not transfer uniformly across metrics or vocabulary granularity, and scope the paper’s headline claims to category-level intent prediction accordingly, leaving a multi-seed, graph-inclusive replication to future work.

sections.heading: V-M Limitations
sections.text: We consolidate the caveats raised individually above: • Single-run headline result. The industrial R@5 gain of + 0.0226 +0.0226 comes from one training run; we estimate variance indirectly via the five-seed MovieLens sweep (Table IX , std = 0.0017 =0.0017 –0.0009 R@5), noting the industrial gap is ≈ 13 \approx 13 – 25 × 25\times that spread as a proxy, not a direct measurement. • The graph ablation is not an independent retrain (Section V-J ): edge definitions are swapped at inference on a shared backbone, not retrained from scratch, so the + 0.0013 +0.0013 R@5 edge is evidence the backbone transfers well to behavioral edges rather than a fully controlled comparison. • The item-level check is preliminary and single-run (Section V-I ): directionally mixed, with no multi-seed estimate to separate a real effect from noise. • The 20-interaction threshold is a chosen operating point, not a discovered constant (Section V-F ): we draw the line where the per-bin gain first reaches ≥ \geq 0.004 R@5, a threshold of practical rather than statistical significance; platforms with a different complexity tolerance could reasonably draw it elsewhere using Table III . • The additional knobs in Section V-H are re-slices of a single run , without independent retraining to attach confidence intervals to individual grid cells.

sections.heading: VI Deployment, Business Impact, and Qualitative Analysis
sections.text: BehaveRec has been live in production since 2025, serving intent-based recommendation carousels on the Item Detail Page (surfacing complementary intent clusters during browsing) and the post-add-to-cart page (basket completion around a coherent mission) – two of the highest-intent surfaces in the shopping journey. The carousel title, generated from the predicted cluster’s human-readable label (Section III-A ), is a key engagement driver.

sections.heading: VII Conclusion
sections.text: We set out to answer a specific question: when does long-term behavioral history, and community-level behavioral signal, actually help sequential recommendation? We built BehaveRec – a three-signal framework combining a causal session transformer, a 90-day bidirectional User History Encoder, and a GraphSAGE module over a behavioral embedding similarity graph, fused via a learned ThreeWayGate – as the instrument for this study. On 137M sequences from 12.6M users, BehaveRec outperforms SASRec and Repeat-Last by the margins reported in Sections V-C and V-D , and a higher-capacity SASRec-Large ablation (Section V-E ) confirms most of this gain is architectural rather than capacity-driven. The more actionable finding is where that gain comes from. A user-level history stratification (Table III ), holding domain and vocabulary fixed, shows a monotonic dose-response relationship with history length – corroborated across four public and industrial datasets (Section V-G ) and by a joint session-length/history-length breakdown (Section V-H ) – yielding a practical operating point of ≈ \approx 20 interactions per user for deployment. This threshold, and the headline numbers above, are established for category-level intent prediction; a preliminary, single-run evaluation on the full item-level MovieLens vocabulary (Section V-I ) shows a directionally mixed result, which we flag as an open question for future multi-seed replication and an explicit boundary on our headline claims. We summarize this and the paper’s other soft spots together in Section V-M . Taken together, we see the paper’s main contribution as the dose-response evidence and the resulting deployment rule (Table III ) rather than the architecture in isolation: practitioners can use it to decide, from their own platform’s history-length distribution, whether long-term behavioral modeling is worth adopting at all.

A Study with Session, History, and Community Signals Aysenur Inan, Reza Yousefi Maragheh, Jayesh Uddhav Kudase, Selene Xu, Kaushiki Nag, Jianpeng Xu, Sushant Kumar Affiliation: Walmart Global Tech, Sunnyvale, CA, USA {aysenur.inan, reza.yousefimaragheh, jayeshuddhav.kudase, yue.xu, kaushiki.nag, jianpeng.xu, sushant.kumar}@walmart.com Abstract Sequential recommendation models typically predict a user’s next action from recent session interactions, which limits personalization when short-term signals are weak or ambiguous. Rather than assuming that incorporating longer-term history and community signals is universally beneficial, we study when it actually helps. We propose BehaveRec, a three-signal framework combining a causal session transformer, a bidirectional User History Encoder (UHE) over a 90-day window, and a GraphSAGE module over a user-user graph built from behavioral embedding similarity rather than item co-occurrence; a learned gate blends the three signals per user. On an industrial dataset of 137M sequences from 12.6M users, BehaveRec improves R@5 by + 3.2 % +3.2\% over SASRec, with a larger-capacity SASRec baseline (more parameters than BehaveRec) still trailing by + 2.5 % +2.5\% , ruling out capacity as the explanation. More importantly, a user-level stratification by history length reveals a clear dose-response relationship: BehaveRec’s advantage is negligible below roughly 10 interactions and grows monotonically with history richness, reaching + 0.017 +0.017 R@5 for users with 101+ events. This pattern is corroborated across one industrial and three public datasets spanning history-rich (MovieLens) to history-sparse (Amazon) regimes, where session-only models remain preferable. These headline results, and the resulting deployment threshold, are established for category-level intent prediction; a preliminary, single-run check on the full item-level vocabulary (Section V-I ) yields a directionally mixed result and is scoped as an open question rather than a claim. We use these results to derive a practical deployment rule – roughly 20 interactions per user – for when long-term history and behavioral-graph signals are worth their added complexity. Despite this added complexity, BehaveRec remains lightweight: it uses 5.67M parameters and trains on a single GPU in under two days. Index Terms: Sequential Recommendation, User History Encoding, Behavioral Graph, History-Richness Threshold, GraphSAGE, Industrial Scale, Intent Prediction I Introduction Recommender systems are central to the user experience of large-scale e-commerce platforms, where predicting a customer’s next intent translates directly to measurable business outcomes. The dominant paradigm for sequential recommendation has converged on self-attention-based models such as SASRec [ 1 ] , which model the causal structure of a user’s recent session to identify the most likely next action. Despite strong aggregate performance, session-only models have a fundamental limitation: they cannot personalize predictions across users who share identical short-term sessions. Consider two customers who both viewed and added a coffee grinder to cart. One is a daily coffee enthusiast with 200 events across coffee equipment and pet dental care; the other is a college student making a one-time purchase. A session-only model assigns both users identical predictions. The session captures what the user is doing right now; it says nothing about who the user is. This gap motivates the integration of longer-term personal history. User behavior over a 90-day window encodes a behavioral persona: recurring clusters of intent, activity patterns, and category affinities that define a user’s preferences independent of any single session. Beyond personal history, behavioral communities offer a complementary signal – users who share similar long-term behavioral personas tend to follow similar transition patterns across intent clusters. Rather than assuming richer history and community signals are always worth their added modeling and serving complexity, we ask a more specific question: when does long-term behavioral history help session-based recommendation, and by how much? Answering this requires an architecture capable of using such signals, controlled comparisons that isolate their marginal contribution, and an evaluation designed to detect the point at which they stop mattering. We build BehaveRec to serve as this instrument, and use it to conduct a user-level and cross-domain study of history-richness effects at industrial scale. As we show, the answer is not “always” or “never” but a quantifiable dose-response curve (Section V-F ) – and we report the cases where the added signal does not help (Sections V-G , V-I ) with the same care as the cases where it does. I-A Limitations of Existing Approaches Session-only models [ 1 , 2 ] operate exclusively on short interaction windows, degrading for cold-session users and multi-category sessions. Graph-based approaches such as LightGCN [ 3 ] model user-item co-purchase graphs, but item co-purchase similarity is a coarse proxy for behavioral similarity: two users who purchased the same item may have fundamentally different behavioral personas and transition tendencies. LLM-based approaches [ 4 ] are impractical for production systems at scales of 137 million training sequences. I-B Our Approach We propose BehaveRec, a three-signal framework encoding: • h short h_{\text{short}} (Session Encoder): A 4-layer causal transformer over the user’s 7-day session, capturing immediate intent. • h long h_{\text{long}} (User History Encoder, UHE): A 4-layer bidirectional transformer with a learnable [USER] token, encoding the 90-day behavioral persona into a single 256-d vector that is user-specific even when sessions are identical. • h graph h_{\text{graph}} (Behavioral Community Signal): A GraphSAGE [ 5 ] aggregation over a user-user graph whose edges reflect behavioral similarity of learned history embeddings – not item co-occurrence. A learned ThreeWayGate blends all three signals per user. BehaveRec is trained with label-smoothed cross-entropy augmented by InfoNCE [ 6 ] contrastive alignment between session and history representations. We use this architecture as a controlled instrument: each signal can be independently disabled, measured, and stratified by user history length, which is what makes the empirical study in Section V-F possible. I-C Contributions • A systematic study of when long-term history and behavioral-graph signals help. A user-level stratification on the industrial test set (Table III , Section V-F ) shows BehaveRec’s advantage over a session-only baseline is negligible below ∼ \sim 10 interactions and grows monotonically with history length, corroborated by a four-dataset cross-domain comparison (Section V-G ) that yields a practical deployment threshold of ≈ \approx 20 interactions per user. • BehaveRec architecture: session encoding, 90-day personal history encoding, and behavioral community graph signal fused via a learned ThreeWayGate. • Behavioral community graph with controlled validation: users are connected via cosine similarity of learned UHE history embeddings rather than item co-occurrence; a controlled ablation (Table VII , Section V-J ) shows this outperforms item co-occurrence edges (LightGCN-style). • Industrial-scale validation with capacity controls: a SASRec-Large ablation (Section V-E ) confirms most of BehaveRec’s gain is architectural rather than a capacity artifact. • An honest account of where the approach does not help: sparse-history Amazon benchmarks (avg 14–17 events) favor SASRec, and a full item-level MovieLens evaluation (Section V-I ) shows a directionally mixed result rather than a uniform win. • Practical scalability: 5.67M parameters, single A100 GPU, under two days – roughly a 1,000 × \times parameter reduction vs. LLM approaches. II Related Work II-A Sequential Recommendation Early approaches used Markov chains and matrix factorization. GRU4Rec [ 7 ] applied recurrent units; Caser [ 8 ] used convolutional filters. SASRec [ 1 ] introduced causal self-attention and remains a standard baseline. BERT4Rec [ 2 ] extended this with bidirectional attention. A common limitation is exclusive reliance on the current session: users sharing identical recent sequences receive identical predictions regardless of differing long-term histories. II-B Graph-Augmented Recommendation LightGCN [ 3 ] propagates embeddings through bipartite user-item graphs. GraphSAGE [ 5 ] , which underlies our graph module, learns inductive aggregation functions suited for production systems with continuous new users. SURGE [ 9 ] builds metric-learned item graphs from sessions for sparse settings. All these approaches build graphs from item co-occurrence or user-item overlap. BehaveRec instead constructs user-user graphs from behavioral similarity of learned 90-day history embeddings, connecting users whose full behavioral patterns are similar rather than users who merely co-purchased an item. II-C LLM-Based Recommendation TALLRec [ 4 ] and CoLLM [ 10 ] fine-tune or augment LLM backbones for recommendation. These approaches are impractical at scales of 137M training sequences and tens of millions of users. BehaveRec achieves comparable architectural goals with 5.67M parameters on a single GPU. II-D Industrial Long-Term User Modeling and User-User Graphs Two lines of prior work are closest to BehaveRec. Industrial long-/short-term systems (MIMN [ 11 ] ; SIM and TWIN [ 12 , 13 ] ; SLi-Rec [ 14 ] ) combine long- and short-term interest via attention or memory networks, but operate over raw item vocabularies through auxiliary retrieval over a sparse subset of historical items; the resulting long-term signal is a re-weighted item history, not a separately learnable user representation. BehaveRec instead encodes the full 90-day window into a single bidirectional embedding over a pre-clustered intent vocabulary and reuses that embedding for both fusion and graph construction. Separately, embedding-based user-user collaborative filtering [ 15 , 16 ] links users by latent-factor or social-tie similarity derived from static rating or co-purchase matrices, so users are connected only if they overlap on items. BehaveRec’s edges instead come from cosine similarity between learned sequential history embeddings produced by the same UHE that drives fusion, so two users with no items in common can still be neighbors if their 90-day transition patterns are similar, and the graph is naturally recomputed as those embeddings drift. We view this combination – one shared history encoder feeding both a fusion signal and an inductive, retraining-free behavioral graph – as architecturally distinct from these two lines of prior work, rather than a straightforward instance of either. We stop short of a claim of established superiority: as noted in Section V-B , we do not benchmark directly against these systems, since they operate at ad-retrieval scale and are not directly portable to our intent-cluster task, so we have no head-to-head number to support a stronger claim here. V-G Cross-Domain Corroboration The within-domain stratification in Table III provides controlled, direct evidence that BehaveRec’s advantage tracks history length. This is corroborated by a coarser, cross-dataset comparison spanning four domains with different vocabularies and item semantics (Table II ). Users with ≥ \geq 20 interactions are, on average, better served by BehaveRec, while users with fewer than 20 interactions are better served by session-only models. On datasets dominated by users above this threshold – industrial dataset ( h ¯ = 119 \bar{h}{=}119 , 89.8% of users ≥ \geq 20 interactions) and MovieLens ( h ¯ = 166 \bar{h}{=}166 , 100% of users ≥ \geq 20 interactions) – BehaveRec consistently outperforms SASRec ( + 3.2 % +3.2\% and + 0.67 % +0.67\% R@5 respectively, Table II ). The five-seed sweep in Table IX confirms this holds across seeds (positive delta on all five, mean + 0.0061 +0.0061 R@5, std 0.0017 0.0017 ); absolute values in that sweep differ slightly from the single run in Table II due to run-to-run variation, but the direction and approximate magnitude of the improvement are consistent. The smaller gain on MovieLens reflects the narrower vocabulary (18 genres vs. 2,371 clusters) and more predictable genre transitions. On Amazon CDs & Vinyl ( h ¯ = 17 \bar{h}{=}17 , 28% of users ≥ \geq 20 interactions) and Electronics ( h ¯ = 14 \bar{h}{=}14 , 15% of users ≥ \geq 20 interactions), the pattern reverses: SASRec outperforms BehaveRec by 4.6 % 4.6\% and 15.9 % 15.9\% relative R@5 ( − 0.0307 -0.0307 and − 0.0311 -0.0311 absolute R@5, respectively). This is consistent with Table III : both Amazon datasets are dominated by users in the 1–10 event range, precisely the regime where the within-domain stratification shows BehaveRec at approximate parity with or slightly below SASRec. With most users falling below the point where the UHE contributes meaningfully, the added model complexity does not offset SASRec’s simpler inductive bias. We flag this as a limitation : BehaveRec is not universally superior; its benefit is conditional on sufficient historical signal, and Table III lets a practitioner estimate the expected gain from their own platform’s history-length distribution rather than relying on a single binary threshold. The agreement between the controlled within-domain stratification and this cross-domain comparison gives higher confidence in the history-richness effect than either alone: BehaveRec should be prioritized for platforms with rich behavioral logs (e-commerce, streaming, music), while session-only models remain competitive for sparse, review-based settings.
